newsitem.title: USA: White House discloses vists by Asian, prompts row.
newsitem.headline: White House discloses vists by Asian, prompts row.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent
The White House disclosed on Wednesday that an Asian tycoon who gave the Democratic Party hundreds of thousands of laundered dollars visited the White House at least 10 times from 1994 to 1996.

The timing of the revelation, coming a day after the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee heard testimony centering on the role of Ng Lap Sing in campaign fund-raising scandals, provoked an angry response from the committee's Republican chairman, Tennessee Sen. Fred Thompson.

It prompted Thompson to suspend his policy of cooperating with the White House to gain access to information. He declared he would issue a blanket subpoena on Thursday for all relevant White House material.
"It is clear that the White House is not cooperating the way they said they would," a furious Thompson told reporters. "We're going to have to follow through with a subpoena which we will tomorrow."

He said the White House was trying to delay, obstruct and confuse his investigation into the way foreign money flowed into the U.S. political system and whether U.S. foreign policy was influenced or its security breached.

The Senate investigation is supposed to conclude on Dec. 21 but Thompson said the development might constitute grounds to extend it. "I would give no credibility at the moment to anything the White House says," he added.

The information from Secret Service records showed Ng, who was also known as Wu, as entering the White House five times to meet Mark Middleton, who was then special assistant to the president and deputy to the White House counsellor.
Another of his visits in February 1995 was to attend a Democratic National Committee dinner addressed by President Bill Clinton. Two were for private tours.

The revelation that Ng had access to the White House is certain to add to Clinton administration embarrassment. He is just the latest in a series of people who seem to have been able to enter the building almost at will.
Ng was the primary Asian contact for Yah Lin "Charlie" Trie, who got to know Clinton when he ran a Chinese restaurant in Little Rock when Clinton was governor of Arkansas.

The committee heard evidence on Tuesday culled from subpoenaed bank records of how Trie received $905,000 from Ng, a Macau-based business tycoon with links to the Chinese government and Communist Party.

The money flowed through six separate accounts established by Trie under a variety of different corporate names. Sometimes he switched funds from account to account several times before it finally wound up in Democratic coffers.

Along with his wife and company, Trie gave $220,000 to the Democratic Party from 1994 to 1996 and tried to give almost $800,000 to Clinton's Presidential Legal Expense Trust, which refused to accept it.

The DNC did take his money but paid it back this year when it became clear it illegally came from overseas. Both Trie and Ng have refused to answer questions about their role and Trie has taken refuge in China.

The committee on Wednesday heard how Trie wrote a letter to Clinton, delivered by Middleton, concerning his view of military tension between China and Taiwan in March 1996 and received a personal reply drafted by National Security Adviser Anthony Lake and signed by the president.
"Charlie Trie is a very typical Asian agent acting on behalf of his sponsor," said Utah Republican Sen. Bob Bennett.
